Provenance receipts

Source: vignettes/receipt.Rmd
receipt.Rmd

A receipt is one JSON file per output that says what the output is, how it was made, what came out, and where and when. Every package and catalogue that publishes a table, raster, model or STAC item is to write its receipts in this one shape, so any rebuild can be compared with a reference copy and answered identical, equivalent within a declared tolerance, or different, naming what differed.

crate holds the contract in a form any language can implement (a JSON Schema, a canonical JSON rule, a fingerprint specification, a register of what each difference does, a mapping from older records, and test vectors) and one R implementation of it. stacs.receipt is a Python implementation for STAC catalogues that runs the same vectors (crate#43, stacs#12). This vignette is the contract’s reference.

library(crate)

Two questions, three answers

A rebuild asks two questions. Was it made the same way? That is the recipe: code, config, the inputs’ identities, a seed. Did it come out the same? That is the result. The same recipe can give slightly different results on another machine or another day, through row order, float summation order, or a model fitted with random draws, so “equivalent” has to be an answer in its own right:

verdict recipe result
identical the same the same
equivalent the same every value that differs is within its declared tolerance
different another or a value past its tolerance

The worked case

One link build’s evidence was built twice from the same code (knowledge#145). Three tables came out byte-identical. The fourth, access_check, had the same rows and counts but differed in the 11th decimal place, at most 9.5e-11 km, because the database summed in another order. crate ships a synthetic copy of the two builds, each with its receipt:

wc <- system.file("extdata", "receipt", "examples", "worked_case", package = "crate")
list.files(file.path(wc, "build_1"))
#> [1] "access_check.csv"   "receipt.json"       "visits_link.csv"   
#> [4] "visits_species.csv" "walks.csv"
read.csv(file.path(wc, "build_1", "access_check.csv"))
#>   segment accessible       km
#> 1    S010       TRUE 12.34568
#> 2    S011       TRUE  3.14000
#> 3    S012      FALSE  0.87500
#> 4    S013       TRUE 31.01610
read.csv(file.path(wc, "build_2", "access_check.csv"))
#>   segment accessible       km
#> 1    S010       TRUE 12.34568
#> 2    S011       TRUE  3.14000
#> 3    S012      FALSE  0.87500
#> 4    S013       TRUE 31.01610

The output declares a tolerance of 1e-9 on km, so both receipts carry the same fingerprint for access_check, and the comparison answers equivalent:

crt_receipt_compare(file.path(wc, "build_1"), file.path(wc, "build_2"))
#> equivalent (receipts only; register v1.0.0)
#>   within result.parts[access_check.csv].bytes: 124 vs 128; table access_check agrees
#>   within result.parts[access_check.csv].sha256: "04994ff01cdee55d69fc410add51ad261ec4b33a751135fc224e97305823c3e2" vs "6801fb7bb092626441fd804d5ffbf8c4c05213ff18fa7c7ca524a9c2aa32f5e4"; table access_check agrees
#>   within result.summary[km_total]: 47.3767792597 vs 47.376779259805; within 1e-06
#>   record context.run: {"link_run_id":"20261104T181900Z-bulk"} vs {"link_run_id":"20261104T214400Z-bulk"}
#>   record context.time: "2026-11-04T18:22:05Z" vs "2026-11-04T21:47:31Z"

access_check.csv’s bytes differ, but the receipt says that file holds the access_check table, whose fingerprint agrees; km_total differs within its 1e-6; the run identifiers and times are context, recorded and never part of an identity.

The four blocks 

r <- crt_receipt_read(file.path(wc, "build_1"))
names(r)
#> [1] "context" "output"  "recipe"  "result"

output: what the thing is. Not hashed.

field
name the output’s name
scope its partition (a watershed group, a region), or null
receipt_version "1.0.0"
schema the crate schema the output conforms to, or null
migrated_from only in a receipt read from an older record

recipe: how it was made. Its identity is recipe_id.

field
code keyed by repository of ours: commit (40 hex), version, dirty
config files (keyed by path: the SHA-256 of its bytes) and settings (the resolved run settings, verbatim)
inputs keyed by input name: exactly one of recipe_id, version_id, sha256, or none (why neither)
seed the seed of any fit, or null
recipe_id SHA-256 over the canonical JSON of the fields above

result: what came out.

field
fingerprint keyed by table: sha256, rows
parts keyed by path relative to the receipt: bytes, sha256, and table where the file holds a fingerprinted table
summary keyed by name: a number (rows, km_total)
tolerance tables (table, then column: a tolerance) and summary (name: a tolerance)

context: where and when. Never part of an identity.

field
time UTC, ISO 8601 with a trailing Z
host optional; left out of a receipt that is published
run, session run identifiers, a note
toolchain third-party versions: R, GDAL, terra, arrow
lockfile_sha256 the SHA-256 of renv.lock, or null
inputs each input’s own result, for reporting
legacy in a migrated receipt, the older record’s fields with no receipt key

The schema is published at https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/crate/receipt/v1.0.0/schema.json and installed with crate. A published version is never edited.

Three parts of the contract are versioned, each on its own (crate#58). The schema is the receipt’s form, and its version is the one a receipt carries in output.receipt_version. The register decides what a difference in each field does to a comparison, and a comparison names the register version it was judged under. The mapping turns an older record into a receipt. A change to the register or the mapping is a new version of that part only: it never moves the number on a receipt, because a receipt’s form has not changed. Each register version covers one form version. The rules and every release are in the changelog.

What goes where, and why

  • Toolchain versions are context; a seed is recipe; resolved run settings are config. A GDAL upgrade alone should read “same recipe” and let the result decide. A different seed draws differently, so it is another recipe. Two runs that differ only in a command-line argument are two recipes.
  • recipe_id hashes each input’s recipe identity, never its result. An input rebuilt equivalently has a new result; folding that into recipe_id would make everything downstream different. Input results go in context.inputs, for reporting.
  • Collections are objects keyed by name, never arrays, because canonical JSON sorts object keys and leaves arrays in the order given: two writers listing the same inputs in another order would otherwise compute two ids.
  • crate owns every part that must agree byte for byte; each package declares what only it knows: which inputs and settings are recipe, which tables are fingerprinted, and their tolerances.

The canonical forms

Everything hashed is hashed as bytes of a declared form, never a language’s serialization.

Canonical JSON

RFC 8785, the JSON Canonicalization Scheme: object keys sorted by their UTF-16 code units; strings escaped only where JSON requires (", \, \b \t \n \f \r, other control characters as \u00xx in lowercase hex); numbers in ECMAScript’s shortest round-trip form, in plain decimal from 1e-7 to 1e21 and in exponent form outside it (1e+21, 1e-7, 333333333.3333333); no whitespace.

Two things trip implementations. Read every JSON number as a double: Python’s json reads 1152921504606846976 as an int, which rfc8785 refuses past 2^53, so parse with parse_int=float. The shortest spelling needs a correctly rounded decimal parser: R’s as.numeric() misread 84% of 200,000 random 17-digit spellings on arm64 macOS, where long double is double, so crate reads candidates back through jsonlite, which uses the C library’s strtod.

recipe_id

The SHA-256, lowercase hex, of the UTF-8 bytes of the canonical JSON of the recipe block without its recipe_id:

r$recipe$recipe_id
#> [1] "b06f982dd07b5e44edf586519e5d6ab60b29715a051c3827fba647230636f977"

The table fingerprint

crt_table_fingerprint() is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {"columns": [...], "rows": [[...], ...]}:

  • Columns are sorted by name as UTF-8 bytes.
  • Every cell is a string, or null for NA. Text is its UTF-8, not normalized; a factor is its label.
  • Integers are their digits; logicals true and false.
  • A double with a declared tolerance 10^-k is written with exactly k decimals, rounding its exact binary value with ties to even, as C’s printf("%.*f") and Python’s format(x, ".kf") do. Without a tolerance it is written in the shortest round-trip form above. A zero has no sign. NaN and infinities are refused.
  • Dates are YYYY-MM-DD; datetimes are UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, and fractional seconds are refused. A subclass of Date or POSIXct, such as data.table’s IDate, is spelled as its base class.
  • Rows are sorted by the UTF-8 bytes of each row’s own canonical JSON.
a <- data.frame(segment = c("s2", "s1"), km = c(7.25, 12.3456789012))
b <- data.frame(km = c(12.3456789012 + 9.5e-11, 7.25), segment = c("s1", "s2"))
crt_table_fingerprint(a) == crt_table_fingerprint(b)
#> [1] FALSE
crt_table_fingerprint(a, c(km = 1e-9)) == crt_table_fingerprint(b, c(km = 1e-9))
#> [1] TRUE

It is not crt_schema_fingerprint(), which hashes a table’s column names and types, never its values.

Tolerances

A tolerance is an absolute power of ten from 1 to 1e-15. It says both how a fingerprint rounds (k decimals for 10^-k) and what the comparison accepts (|a - b| <= 10^-k). A tolerance that is not a power of ten has no rounding that matches it, and is refused.

Writing a receipt

A package declares, as YAML beside its writer, what only it knows:

# The receipt declaration for the worked case's output (crate#43): what only the
# producing package knows. crt_receipt_keys() reads it.
receipt_keys: 1
output: link_evidence
recipe:
  config_files: [settings.csv]
  settings: [species, watershed_group]
  inputs: [flow, fwa_stream_networks]
  seed: false
result:
  tables:
    access_check:
      tolerance: {km: 1.0e-9}
    visits_link: {}
    visits_species: {}
    walks: {}
  summary:
    rows: {}
    km_total: {tolerance: 1.0e-6}

and hands the writer its values. crt_receipt_write() computes the ids, fingerprints and digests, fills the context, and writes receipt.json atomically:

dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "evidence")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
access <- read.csv(file.path(wc, "build_1", "access_check.csv"))
write.csv(access, file.path(dir, "access_check.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

w <- crt_receipt_write(
  dir,
  output = list(name = "access_check", scope = "BULK"),
  recipe = list(
    code = list(link = list(commit = "a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a7b6c5d4e3f2a1b0",
                            version = "0.31.2", dirty = FALSE)),
    config = list(settings = list(species = c("CO", "CH", "ST"))),
    inputs = list(fwa_stream_networks = list(version_id = "3HL4kqtJlcpXroDTDmJ.rmSpXd3dIbrHY"))
  ),
  result = list(
    tables = list(access_check = access),
    parts = c(access_check = "access_check.csv"),
    summary = list(rows = nrow(access), km_total = sum(access$km)),
    tolerance = list(tables = list(access_check = list(km = 1e-9)),
                     summary = list(km_total = 1e-6))
  ),
  publish = TRUE
)
w$result$fingerprint
#> $access_check
#> $access_check$sha256
#> [1] "ac3a4b6d2811f6eb530a3d2a70a6cdfe226b652d33d2f20f9744560cb67c31d9"
#> 
#> $access_check$rows
#> [1] 4

Name each part by the table it holds. A file whose bytes differ between builds is equivalent only when its table’s fingerprint agrees; a file that names no table, such as a raster nobody fingerprinted, is different.

crt_receipt_validate(file.path(dir, "receipt.json"))

Comparing

crt_receipt_compare() reads the receipt register, one row per field, to decide what a difference in each does: refuse makes the verdict different, warn is reported without changing it, and record is listed only. Every recipe field refuses, because recipe_id covers it; every context field is recorded. Register v1.0.0 is published at https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/crate/receipt/register/v1.0.0/register.csv and installed with crate, and every comparison names the version it read, with any field a package’s declaration overrode.

reg <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "receipt", "register", "v1.0.0", "register.csv",
                            package = "crate", mustWork = TRUE))
table(reg$action)
#> 
#> record refuse   warn 
#>      9     31      3
head(reg[, c("field", "action")], 8)
#>                    field action
#> 1            output.name refuse
#> 2           output.scope refuse
#> 3 output.receipt_version   warn
#> 4          output.schema   warn
#> 5   output.migrated_from   warn
#> 6            recipe.code refuse
#> 7   recipe.code.*.commit refuse
#> 8  recipe.code.*.version refuse

A comparison of receipts alone certifies less than one that re-reads the result. Two values within tolerance can still round apart at the edge (0.0000000014 and 0.0000000016 under 1e-9 round to 0.000000001 and 0.000000002), and the receipts then disagree. Supply both builds’ tables and the comparison checks each against its own receipt, compares their cells, and reports which it did:

tables <- function(build) {
  list(access_check = read.csv(file.path(wc, build, "access_check.csv")))
}
crt_receipt_compare(file.path(wc, "build_1"), file.path(wc, "build_2"),
                    tables = list(a = tables("build_1"), b = tables("build_2")))$mode
#> [1] "bytes"

Older records

crt_receipt_migrate() reads a record written before its package moved to receipts through the mapping table, so it stays readable while writers converge forward, each when it is next touched. Mapping v1.0.0 is published at https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/crate/receipt/mapping/v1.0.0/mapping.csv and installed with crate. A migrated receipt claims no recipe identity, and keeps what it cannot place in context.legacy:

old <- system.file("extdata", "receipt", "examples", "legacy", "link_manifest.json",
                   package = "crate")
m <- crt_receipt_migrate(old, "link manifest.json")
m$recipe
#> $code
#> $code$link
#> $code$link$version
#> [1] "0.31.2"
#> 
#> $code$link$commit
#> [1] "a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a7b6c5d4e3f2a1b0"
#> 
#> $code$link$dirty
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $recipe_id
#> NULL
names(m$context$legacy)
#> [1] "manifest_version" "datasets"         "configs"          "parts"           
#> [5] "files"

The mapping table also lists STAC’s own keys beside the receipt keys they mirror: a part’s sha256 is file:checksum, its bytes file:size, the producing software processing:software, the time processing:datetime. A receipt’s recipe_id goes on an item as receipt:recipe_id, whose field schema crate publishes at https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/crate/stac/receipt/v1.0.0/schema.json.

Test vectors

Every implementation runs the files in inst/extdata/receipt/vectors/v1.0.0/ and must produce each expected value byte for byte: number spellings, canonical JSON, recipe_ids and table fingerprints. These test the hashing, which the form defines, so they are versioned with the form. Doubles are given as IEEE 754 bits, so no decimal parser stands between a vector and its value.

vec <- system.file("extdata", "receipt", "vectors", "v1.0.0", package = "crate", mustWork = TRUE)
list.files(vec)
#> [1] "fingerprint.json" "jcs.json"         "numbers.json"     "README.md"       
#> [5] "recipe_id.json"

Receipt pairs with their verdicts test the register, so they sit with it, in inst/extdata/receipt/register/v1.0.0/compare.json:

reg_dir <- system.file("extdata", "receipt", "register", "v1.0.0", package = "crate",
                       mustWork = TRUE)
list.files(reg_dir)
#> [1] "compare.json" "README.md"    "register.csv"
